en: The Commentary on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, Together with its Preface, composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gushan.
As for the essence of the nature of mind, it is luminous! It is tranquil! It is simply one. There is no ordinary being...

In its ultimate reality, it has no dependence or correctness, no extension or brevity, and no purity or defilement; yet when it is stirred by responding to things and transforms according to conditions, it becomes the six classes of ordinary beings or the three ranks of sages, possessing both dependence and correctness.
Once the primary and secondary environments have been fashioned, there arise extensions or shortenings of lifespan, as well as purity or defilement of the lands!

Our Buddha, the Great Sage, attained the essence of clarity and stillness; yet he took the path of compassion and made his dwelling in pity. Wishing to drive away the masses of deluded beings and cause them to return to their original nature, he manifested bodies where there was no body and manifested lands where there was no land. He extended his lifespan and purified his land to inspire those who were weary of brevity and impurity; he shortened his lifespan and defiled his land to inspire those who craved longevity and purity. Once they felt both inspiration and weariness, the strategy of gradual guidance could be put into practice.
Therefore, Śākyamuni manifests with measure and takes up a defiled land; is this not because he wishes to cause others to feel weary of the world?
Amitābha manifests as immeasurable and takes up a pure land; is this not because he wishes to cause others to feel joyful aspiration?

This involves breaking down that which is rigid and gathering in that which is scattered, so as to cause beings to return to their original state and realize their nature. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"To take up a Buddha-land according to the means by which sentient beings are to be tamed"—is this not precisely what is meant?

Although the jeweled towers and golden grounds lack objects for visual delight, they do not consist of seductive or distracting colors, thereby enabling one to realize that there is only mind and no external objects.

Although the sounds of wind in the trees and birds have the pleasure of entering the ears, they do not consist of discordant or jarring tones, thereby enabling one to maintain mindfulness of the Three Jewels as one’s refuge.
In this way, returning to the essence of luminous stillness is as easy as turning over one's palm.
As the Sūtra says:
"All sentient beings who are born are already *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive)."
How great indeed!
Such is the skillful mastery of the Sage.
Therefore, although the various scriptures stand in array, they each extol the Pure Land; how profound their underlying intent is!
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha—is this not what is called "partial praise"?

I cherish its words for being concise yet clear in principle, and its prose for being succinct yet complete in substance; it is sufficient to entice those who have strayed since childhood and to awaken the ignorant.

Thus, adhering to the school of Nāgārjuna and following the teachings of the Wise One (Chih-i), I have composed this commentary on the meaning by investigating the principles according to the sūtras. As for the most profound refinements of subtle mysteries, how could I presume to do so? My hope is merely that it may assist the true tradition and provide benefit for future generations.
The explanation of the title according to the fivefold profound meaning (*xuanyi*) consists of:
"Two Lands," which refers to the names of the fruition-stage persons;
and "Vaipulya" (*fangdeng*), which refers to the essence of the true mark (*shixiang*).
Faith and aspiration are the essence of the Pure Land school;
abandoning suffering and attaining bliss is its function;
and being born in the Pure Land is the teaching of the Mahāyāna.

Now, names serve to explain the essence, and one realizes the essence through the central tenet; once the tenet is established, it possesses utility, and thus the four meanings are arranged in sequence.
Since the distinctions between the Great and Small Vehicles have not yet been discerned, it is necessary to differentiate them by means of the characteristics of their teachings.

Regarding the names of the first six characters, there are both general and specific applications: the character "sūtra" (經) is a general name, as it is a designation shared by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
the preceding five characters are specific names, as they distinguish this [text] from others.
Regarding these distinct names, "Buddha" is the general designation for one who has attained the fruit, while "Amitābha" is the specific title of that particular person who has attained the fruit.
Since Śākyamuni is the Lord of Transformation in this land and is known by all sentient beings, his specific name is concealed and his general title is emphasized.
Since Amitābha is the World-Honored One of that land, it is necessary to distinguish him clearly; therefore, his general title is abbreviated and his specific name is retained.
The mutual manifestation of the general and the specific makes their meaning perfectly clear.
To summarize them comprehensively, there are three pairs:
the "Sūtra" refers to the teaching that expresses, while the "above" refers to the meaning expressed; this is the pair of teaching and meaning.
"Amitābha" designates the World-Honored One of that land, while "Buddha" refers to the Transformation Lord of this realm; these two are paired as subject and object.
"Speaking" refers to the truthful vocal karma, and "Buddha" refers to the golden-colored physical body; these two are paired as body and speech.
Within this breadth and narrowness, three pairs of opposites reside therein.

"Buddha" is the sublime title for the ultimate fruition; fruition must necessarily be achieved through causes. That which initiates awakening is termed the cause; awakening must necessarily proceed from delusion—for if there were no delusion, how could there be awakening?
Delusion is not fundamentally real; from where, then, could awakening arise?
If one wishes to clarify this principle, one must understand the six levels of "thusness":
first, the Buddha as suchness (li-ji fo).
2. Buddhahood as Name; 3. Buddhahood as Contemplative Practice;
4. Buddhahood as Resemblance;
Fifth, the partially realized Buddha;
sixth, the ultimately perfected Buddha.
There are six because ordinary beings and sages are not conflated; they are termed "identical" because both the initial and final stages are the Buddha-nature itself.

Regarding "the principle is itself the Buddha": the single thought-moment is the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Because it is as-it-is (*tathatā*), it is emptiness; because it is a treasury (*garbha*), it is the provisional; because it is the principle, it is the Middle. Thus, the three wisdoms are primordially complete within a single mind, not merely acquired now; this is called "the principle is itself the Buddha."

Regarding "the name itself is the Buddha": although in principle it is indeed so, one does not know it for oneself because one has not yet heard of the Three Truths and does not recognize the Buddha-dharma—just as the eyes of cattle and sheep do not recognize the cardinal directions. However, if through a spiritual friend or a scriptural volume one hears what has been explained above, one attains thorough understanding and penetration regarding the name, knowing that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma; this is called "the name itself is the Buddha."

Regarding those who attain Buddhahood through contemplative practice: if one merely hears the names or speaks them aloud, it is like an insect eating wood that happens to form characters; this insect does not know whether these are characters or not. Since there is no comprehension, how could this be Bodhi?

One must have clear mental visualization and accord with the wisdom of principle; one's actions must correspond to one's words, and one's words must correspond to one's actions. When speech and conduct are in harmony, this is called "contemplative practice is itself the Buddha."

Regarding "resemblance to Buddhahood": the more one contemplates, the clearer it becomes; the more one brings [the mind] to rest, the more tranquil it becomes. Coarse defilements fall away of their own accord, and the six sense faculties mutually [attain] realization, like brass resembling gold or a precious pearl where the color and form are similar; this is called resemblance to Buddhahood.

Regarding "partial realization of Buddhahood" (*fen zhen ji fo*): by means of a semblance contemplation, one enters the stage of the first abode (*prathamā bhūmi*), shatters ignorance, perceives the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), opens the secret treasury, and manifests *tathatā*. From the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāyogi-bodhi*), one may manifest universally across the nine realms to benefit sentient beings, or achieve the path through the eight phases (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*) to deliver beings with the Buddha-body; this is termed "partial realization of Buddhahood."

Regarding "the ultimate is itself Buddhahood": from the mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), one enters into Sublime Enlightenment (*tathāgata-jñāna*). The light of wisdom is perfected and can no longer increase; the darkness of delusion is extinguished and there is nothing further to be severed. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can know this; it is called the ultimate being itself Buddhahood.

It is like a poor man who possesses a treasure but is unaware of it; when a wise friend points it out to him, he then becomes aware of it. Thereupon, he weeds away the grass and filth and digs it up; gradually drawing closer to it, once he has drawn near, he opens the storehouse, takes it all, and by using it, attains great wealth and happiness.
By means of this analogy for the six stages of identity (*liujie*), its essential meaning becomes clear.

When we now speak of the Buddha, we refer to Śākyamuni, the Lord of Transformation, who is the person of ultimate perfection. To understand it in this way is not only to recognize that the sublimity of the fruit-stage must necessarily be achieved through causes, but it also leads one to realize that the subtle and wondrous nature of the fruit is inherently present within one's own mind. Thus, at the beginning, as an ordinary person, one possesses the principle and proceeds toward realization without timidity; at the end, as a sage, one abides in Buddhahood and no conceit arises.
"Shuo" (to speak) means "delight" (*yue*); to speak according to the capacity of the listener is called "delighting.

When the Buddha cherishes this sutra, he immediately attains the capacity of those beings; for those who have a karmic affinity with Amitābha, he praises that land’s environment and its inhabitants to inspire them to make vows for rebirth there. Once born in that realm, they will never regress and will ultimately attain Bodhi—this is called "delight," and it is precisely here that the Buddha resides.
*Amitābha* is a Sanskrit term; here it signifies "immeasurable. *A* means "no," and *mitābha* means "measure.
For what reason is it named "Immeasurable"?
It is named for four reasons:
first, its radiant illumination is immeasurable;
second, the limit of its lifespan is immeasurable.
Third, his great and small disciples are immeasurable;
fourth, those in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*) are immeasurable. Based on these four matters, he is established with the honorific title [of Immeasurable].
That various sutras translate this as "Buddha of Immeasurable Life" is merely one of the meanings listed below; all four meanings are present within the text of the sutra.
Now, all Buddhas possess both the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), and thus there are two kinds of immeasurability:
first, the immeasurability of the birth-body, which is the "immeasurable within the measurable";
second, the immeasurability of the dharma-body, which is the "immeasurable within the immeasurable."

The Dharma-body is likened to space, being without birth or extinction; the birth-body is like the moon reflected in water, appearing and disappearing. Thus, both Śākyamuni and Amitābha equally attain the infinity of the Dharma-body. However, because the capacities of those in this land are inferior, they perceive the birth-body as finite; whereas because the faculties of those in that land are superior, they perceive the birth-body as infinite. This "infinity" is spoken of only because it cannot be counted by humans or devas; yet, when compared with the Dharma-body, it certainly belongs to the realm of the finite.
One should know that Śākyamuni is also able to manifest immeasurable [lands] to take hold of a pure land, and Amitābha is also able to manifest measurable [lands] to take hold of a defiled land.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Śākyamuni Buddha has further pure lands, such as the land of Amitābha Buddha."
Amitābha Buddha likewise possesses an impure land, just as the land of Śākyamuni Buddha does.
It is further said:
because this Jambudvīpa is defiled, the Buddha’s lifespan here must be short; because other places are excellent, the Buddha’s lifespan there must be long.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Thirty-two Ganges-sands of world-systems to the west of here lies the land called Unsurpassed Victory (*Anabhibhūta*). Its adornments are like those of the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), and it is there that I appear in the world."
Is this not the manifestation of purity by Śākyamuni?
The *Drum-Sound King Sūtra* states:
"Amitābha Buddha was of the Brahmin caste; his mother’s name was Viśeṣamukhā, and he also had a rebellious disciple named Devadatta."
Since there are women and those who commit heinous crimes, is it not the case that Amitābha manifests a defiled realm?
Thus we know that the birth-bodies of both Buddhas are each twofold; whether they manifest purity or defilement differs according to conditions.
Question:

"Since Śākyamuni himself is able to manifest a pure land, why does he not encourage sentient beings to make vows to be reborn there, but instead delivers them by sending them to the land of Amitābha?"
The answer is:
"Because the capacities of sentient beings are not equal, the means of transformation are likewise diverse.

If one has a karmic affinity for only a single Buddha, they are transformed by that Buddha from beginning to end. If one has affinities for two Buddhas, they are transformed by both together. Therefore, Śākyamuni manifests an impure land to subdue them, while Amitābha manifests a pure land to gather them in; through this simultaneous subduing and gathering, sentient beings are ripened together until they reach Bodhi."
Question: "The Dharma of a Bodhisattva should be to deliver sentient beings; why then do they seek only a land of bliss? Answer:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 43, contains this question, to which Nāgārjuna replies:
"There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
the first are those who, with a preponderance of compassion, act for the sake of sentient beings."
Second, they extensively accumulate the merits of all Buddhas.

Those who delight in extensively accumulating merit reach the pure land of Infinite Life of the One Vehicle; those who prefer to act for the sake of sentient beings reach places where there is no Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha to proclaim the sound of praise for the Triple Gem.
Question: "If that is so, would it not follow that one who delights in accumulating merit would fail to transform sentient beings? Answer:
"It is not so; it is merely a difference of sequence.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 45, further states:

'Among bodhisattvas, there are those who first accomplish their own merits and virtues and subsequently deliver sentient beings, and there are those who first bring sentient beings to accomplishment and subsequently accomplish their own merits and virtues.'"

Regarding "Sūtra": the Sanskrit term is *sūtra*. Translated according to its meaning, it is called "Scripture in Accordance with Truth" (*qìjīng*). This signifies that the expressed principles and meanings accord with the human mind; that is to say, they accord with both the truth and the capacity of the audience.
Regarding the term "sūtra," the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

It is called a sūtra because it can thread together and encompass; for the holy teachings of the Buddha thread together the meanings that ought to be explained and sustain those beings who are to be converted.
The explanation of the names is concluded. Second, regarding the discernment of the essence: the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the Vaipulya constitutes the primary essence of this sutra.

"Vaipulya" means "vast" (*vaipulya*), and "equal" (*sama*) means "equality. Because the essence of true reality extends horizontally across all phenomena, it is called "vast"; because it vertically encompasses both the ordinary and the sage, it is called "equal. Thus, the entire Mahayana of perfect fusion is termed Vaipulya.
However, since the Deer Park had consistently taught only the Small Vehicle until twelve years later when this principle was first expounded, it specifically received that name.
Thus, the *Anantamukha-sādhaka* states:
"Next, he preached the Vaipulya and the Mahāprajñāpāramitā."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"From curd is produced fresh butter; this is a metaphor for how from the *Sūtras* emerge the Vaipulya scriptures. Both of these refer to the third period [of the Buddha's teaching].
Since this sutra belongs to the category of "clarified butter" (ghṛta), it is appropriate to explain its essence by means of this name.

One should know that Amitābha’s adornments of the environment and the inhabitants arise because he has thoroughly manifested this essence; and that sentient beings attain birth [in his land] simply through their aspiration because they inherently possess this essence by principle. Is it not here that the vastness and equality [of the Mahāyāna] reside?
Thus, the substance of its meaning has three aspects:
namely, the meaning of the fundamental substance (*zhuti*), the meaning of the foundation (*di*), and the meaning of penetration (*da*).

Since it serves as the basis for the four chapters and the destination of the three divisions—let alone being the sovereign and subjects of the four classes of people and comparable to the three luminaries adorning the heavens—this is the meaning of the fundamental substance.

If the cause and effect of the Mahāyāna are none other than the true mark (dharmatā), and the great ocean of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) can only be fathomed by a Buddha—this is the sense in which the essence is "the bottom" (tī).

If Prajñā is a single dharma yet the Buddha speaks of it under various names, and the true mark is likewise given many different titles and appellations—this is the sense in which the essence is "penetration" (praveśa).
The explanation of the substance is concluded.
Third, regarding the clarification of the essence (*mūla*): faith, aspiration, and pure practice constitute the essential purport of this sutra.

Now, "essence" refers to that which is fundamental; various and manifold practices are subsumed under the term "cause," and immeasurable merits are subsumed under the term "fruit. One should know that both cause and fruit are equally the essential core.
The Sūtra states:
"One should make a vow to be born in that land.
This clarifies the cause.
It further states:
"Those who hear this sutra and accept and uphold it shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This clarifies the fruit [of the practice]."
Although both meanings are present, the cause is primary and the fruit secondary, because the primary purpose is to exhort practitioners to seek rebirth there.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
"If there are those with faith, they should make a vow to be born in that land."
Furthermore, it is said:
"Upon hearing the teaching that by upholding the name of Amitābha Buddha for even as few as seven days, one shall attain rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Therefore, faith, aspiration, and pure karma are established as the core principles."

The clarification of the essential principle is concluded. Fourth, regarding the function (*yòng*) of this scripture: its function consists in the relinquishing of suffering and the attainment of bliss.

"Function" refers to efficacious power; by practicing in accordance with the words, one is able to relinquish the manifold sufferings of this world and attain the ultimate bliss of that land—this is the efficacious power of this scripture.
The discussion on application is concluded.
Fifth, regarding the classification of the teachings (*jiao*), there are again two parts:
first, the distinction based on the flavor of the teaching (*jiaowei*).
2. The Origin of the Commentary on the Sūtra.

Regarding the first point: since this sūtra was preached specifically to address the śrāvaka disciples, it is verified not to be the "initial milk" taught all at once; yet, as it speaks of sentient beings attaining Buddhahood, how could it be the "curd-flavor" of the Hīnayāna?
Furthermore, because it does not teach that all phenomena are empty, it is not the "ripe ghee" of Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, because it does not open the assembly for the two vehicles, it differs from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*; its teachings and texts are authentic and substantial, corresponding to the third turning of the wheel, the Vaipulya Mahāyāna.

Examining the scope of what is encouraged therein, it encompasses those in the realms of humans and devas as well as the beginners of the four teachings. When compared with the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the latter concerns fixed karma while this concerns only dispersed goodness; the former addresses those of the perfect capacity, whereas this applies universally to both the partial and gradual vehicles.

Regarding the attainment of birth, the treatise merely states that one attains rebirth by having a non-perverted mind; how could this be the same as ascending a diamond platform to realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?

Regarding the description of adornment, it merely states that the flowers are like chariot wheels; how could this be the same as flowers whose petals, even the smallest, measure twenty-five *yojanas* in length and breadth?
By observing this, their relative superiority and inferiority can be known.
Second, regarding the origins of the sutra commentaries: there are two translations of this sutra, one old and one new.
The first is the old translation by Dharma Master Kumārajīva of the Qin dynasty, titled the *Buddhabhāṣita Amitābha Sūtra*.
1. Newly translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty, titled *The Sūtra of the Buddha’s Acceptance through the Praise of the Pure Land*.
The title established in the Qin edition was based on the scripture itself:
"Just as I now praise the benefits of the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha."
The title established by the Tang edition follows the scripture itself, which states:
"One should believe this is the Sutra on the Praise of the Inconceivable Merit and Virtue and the Protection and Mindfulness of All Buddhas."

"Guarding and mindful remembrance" (*anurakṣaṇā*) is merely another name for "gathering and receiving" (*parigraha*); thus, one knows that each of the two translations establishes its title with textual evidence.
What I have now explained is the version from the Qin dynasty.

As for the origin of this commentary: I, being unworthy, have studied the Way of Tiantai and vowed to compose ten commentaries using the method of the Three Contemplations (*sanguan*) to expound upon the ten sutras, thereby serving as a means for the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

The work of revision and editing had already reached seven parts when I fell ill and remained bedridden for years. Fearing that the spark of a stone fire would not last long and that the shadow passing through a crevice is difficult to detain, I felt I was failing my former resolve; thus, supporting my frail body and leaning against a small table, I completed the remaining three parts—namely, the *Anantamukha-sādhaka*, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna*, and this present sutra.

In each of those two commentaries, there is a chapter titled "Origination through Causes. This text was inked upon the brush on the final day of the tenth month in the fifth year of the Tianxi era of the Great Song (the Xin-you year), and the pen was laid down after noon on the second day of the eleventh month.
Although these words and principles are devoid of merit, I hope they may fulfill my original vow and serve as a preliminary introduction for rebirth in the Pure Land.
Now that the ten commentaries are complete, how much longer will this single life last? What relevance have these bodies like empty flowers or these words like echoes in a valley to me?
At that time, I was forty-six years of age.
There was a commentary on the *Amitābha Sūtra* that had been transmitted from Japan, which claimed it was the teaching of Zhiyi; this is incorrect.
The phrasing is colloquial and the meaning is sparse; it is surely a fabrication by the Japanese!
The section on the judgment of teachings concludes. The exegesis of the sutras is divided into three parts:
First, from "Thus have I heard" until the listing of the assembly constitutes the introduction;
second, from "At that time" until "born in that land" constitutes the main body;
third, from "Śāriputra, as I am now" until the end of the sutra constitutes the dissemination.

All sutras possess both a general (tong) and a specific (bie) introduction; they are called "general" because six factors are common to all, and "specific" because the initiating circumstances differ.
This sutra preserves the general introduction but lacks the specific one.
Question:

“The Buddha has stated that all sutras have a prologue—whether it be due to the offering of a parasol, the emission of light, the conclusion of a meal and the gathering of robes, or the arising from meditation at the hour of *prahāṇa*. Why is there no such introductory occasion for this sutra?”

Answer: "Indeed, whenever the Great Sage established a model, there was always a specific occasion for its origin; however, as these matters were not particularly extraordinary, the translators omitted them and did not record them. Why is this so?"

Because this assembly has gathered, it is known that they will certainly request the Dharma; for this reason, the Tathāgata speaks spontaneously without being asked. One should understand that the purpose of gathering the assembly includes both the act of convening them and the initiation [of the teaching].
In the new translation, these words are present; thus, at the conclusion of the assembly in that sutra, it says:
"They have all come together to this seat for the sake of hearing the Dharma."
It is so. Since all the sūtras contain these six matters, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda asked:
"What words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras?"
He replied: "One should say:
'Thus have I heard: the Buddha was dwelling in a certain country together with a great assembly and so forth.
Is it only I who am thus?"
"The sūtras of all Buddhas of the three periods of time all begin in this manner.
Now, in explaining these six matters, they shall be divided into two parts:
the first three clarify Ānanda, and the latter three manifest the Master.
Regarding the first three [characteristics]: first, Ānanda indicates what was heard, as expressed by "Thus";
second, Ānanda reveals the capacity to hear, as expressed by "I heard."
Third, Ānanda refers to the time of hearing because it occurs simultaneously.
As for the latter three [points]:
first, he invokes the beautiful title of the Teacher of the Doctrine, for he is the Buddha;
Second, it clarifies the dwelling place of the Teacher, as he resided in places such as Śrāvastī;
third, it indicates the assembly of the Transformation Master’s disciples, as he was with the great bhikṣus and others.
Although these two points are distinct, they ultimately serve to establish Ānanda’s testimony and faith.

Regarding the phrase "Thus" (evam): the principle of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is without duality and accords with suchness; it is called "thus" because it transcends the hundred negations. Since the sūtra elucidates this principle, it says "Thus."

Furthermore, "thus" (*evam*) is a term used to point to a specific matter; it means that this teaching of the Pure Land was personally heard by me. Therefore, the subsequent phrase states, "I have heard."
Regarding "I who hear," there are three kinds of "I":
first, view; second, pride; [and third, self-identity].
Third, regarding the name:

Ānanda was already an *aśaikṣa* (one beyond training) at the time of the council; thus, his views and conceit were both exhausted. Nevertheless, for the sake of transmitting and transforming [the Dharma], he conformed to worldly conventions and referred to himself as "I."
Regarding "hearing," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

when the faculty of the ear is unimpaired and the sound is within the range of audibility, through the conjunction of these conditions and the mental application (*manasikāra*) of the desire to hear, one hears.
In that case, the principle is originally beyond hearing; it is only in accordance with worldly convention that it is called "hearing.

As for the term "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), this refers to the teaching of such a Pure Land, stating: "I heard [this] on such a year, such a month, and such a day. However, the reason years and so forth are not mentioned and only "at one time" is said is because the temporal systems established by various kings differ from one another.
Just as there are four seasons here in this land, there are three periods there;

in the eastern lands of China, the new moon is considered the first day of the month, whereas in the western land of India, the full moon is considered the first day of the month. If such is the case between these two regions, it can be inferred that the same applies to the four barbarian tribes.
Since it is difficult to determine with certainty, it is therefore generally referred to as "at one time.

As for the term "Buddha," while the Dharma may be taught by four types of persons, here it specifically indicates what was heard directly from the Buddha himself, and not from his disciples, various sages, devas, or emanated beings.

In the language of India, *buddha* is translated here as "the Awakened One" (*jùézhě*). This means that one has ultimately awakened to and realized that all phenomena are nothing other than mind; because such a person has attained this realization, they are called "the Awakened One."
"Regarding 'in Śrāvastī and so forth,' this means that I heard from the Buddha that there was such a place; it refers to hearing the Buddha's teaching at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī.
'In' (zài) signifies dwelling."
The Tathāgata fundamentally abides in the realm of tranquil light; out of compassion for sentient beings, he traces his presence in Śrāvastī.

In the Sanskrit language, Śrāvastī is translated here as "Hearing of Things," meaning that it is a place where the objects of sensory desire and material wealth are fully present, and where people hear and understand liberation.
Regarding "the Jeta Grove" and so forth: these refer to the trees donated by Prince Jeta and the park donated by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
"Jeta" translates as "Victorious in Battle. When the Prince was born, King Prasenajit was victorious in battle against a foreign nation; therefore, he was given that name.

"Anāthapiṇḍada" is a term of this region; in Sanskrit it is called Sudatta, which translates as "Good Giver. Because he practiced giving with excellence, his fellow countrymen praised him and named him Anāthapiṇḍada (Giver to the Destitute).

"One who is young and without a father is called an orphan (*gu*); one who is old and without a son is called solitary (*du*). For this reason, those of high status always provide alms to such persons.
That the tree is planted first and the garden follows is because the ruler is honored and the minister is subordinate."
"Accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus" refers to his retinue.

Ānanda meant that he had not heard this alone in Jeta’s Grove; rather, since the Buddha dwells together with śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and the various hosts of devas and humans, he was present among them and likewise received the teaching.
The reason these six matters are interdependent is that Ānanda’s intention was to transmit what is erroneous or non-erroneous so as to inspire faith in sentient beings.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the assembly of śrāvakas;...
Second, the bodhisattvas;
third, the miscellaneous assembly.
In terms of appearance and attire, the śrāvakas wear conical caps and saffron robes and always sit by the Buddha’s side; therefore, they are mentioned first.
The Bodhisattva adapts to the capacities of beings, and thus his outward manifestations are not constant; therefore, he is placed next [to the Śrāvaka].
Because the bodies of humans and devas do not transcend the mundane world, they are placed last.
Sentient beings perceive only his traces and cannot fathom his fundamental nature; thus, they distinguish superiority and inferiority based on physical form and attire.

If we consider it from the perspective of the internal mind, the śrāvakas sink into emptiness, humans and devas cling to existence, and bodhisattvas follow the Middle Way; therefore, they are listed between the "eldest" and the "youngest" to represent this distinction.
The assembly of śrāvakas is divided into six parts:
first, clarifying their categories;
second, indicating their numbers.
Third, manifesting their status;
fourth, extolling their virtues;
fifth, listing their names.
Sixth, the summary.
"Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus" clarifies their category.
"Together with" (yǔ) means "with" (gòng).
The term "Great" (Mahā) in Sanskrit contains three meanings: greatness, abundance, and excellence.

These venerable masters are called "Great" because they are revered by great beings such as celestial kings; they are called "Abundant" because they have extensively mastered both internal (Buddhist) and external (non-Buddhist) scriptures; and they are called "Excellence" because they transcend the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths. The translator has translated this term based on a single specific meaning.

Regarding the bhikṣu, there are six meanings concerning cause and effect: as for the causes, they are named "mendicant" (bhikṣu), "terrorizer of Māra," and "destroyer of evil"; as for the effects, they are titled "worthy of offerings" (arhat), "slayer of thieves," and "one who does not arise again" (anupapatti).
"Alms-seeker" (bhikṣu) means that one requests [food] to sustain the body and is forever free from the four kinds of improper food.
"Terrifier of Māras" means that when one resolves to leave the household life, the King Māra fears that [the practitioner] will transcend his realm.
"Destroyers of Evil" refers to their ability to destroy the ninety-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*), which are the causes of affliction and evil.
Those listed here among the assembly of fellow disciples are all great Arhats; although their names belong to the causal stage, they are in fact persons who have attained the fruit.

"Seng" (Saṃgha), in its full form, is *saṃgha*; this translates as "the harmony of the assembly. It refers to a group of four or more, up to an infinite number, who demonstrate the two types of harmony—of both phenomena and principle—and are free from conflict or dispute; thus, it is called an "assembly."
"The company of one thousand two hundred and fifty people" indicates the number.

After the Buddha first attained enlightenment and finished delivering the five bhikṣus, he then converted the three Kāśyapas—namely Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, and Nadī-Kāśyapa—who together with their brothers had one thousand disciples.

Next, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were converted; together they had two hundred and fifty disciples, all of whom turned away from heterodoxy toward the Right Path and attained the supreme fruit. Out of gratitude for the Buddha’s kindness, they constantly attended upon him as his attendants.
Furthermore, the *Lalitavistara* states:

"The reason many sūtras enumerate one thousand two hundred and fifty followers is that the compilers of the scriptures listed them out of respect for their being the first to take refuge in the Buddha; it does not necessarily mean they were all present at the assembly."
"All are great Arhats" indicates their eminent status;
that is to say, these bhikṣus are not practitioners still in training (śaikṣa), but have all attained the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
The term "Arhat" encompasses three meanings:
First, Arhat (Worthy One): because they are worthy of being a field of merit for humans and devas, this is the fruit of the mendicant;
second, Kṣīṇāsrava (Destroyer of Thieves): because they have completely severed all afflictions, this is the fruit of overcoming evil;
third, Anupapatti (Non-arising): because they will not undergo further existence, this is the fruit of terrifying Māra.

"Known by the multitude" refers to the praising of his virtues; "knowing" means to admire one's virtue upon hearing their name, while "recognizing" means to reverently honor them upon seeing their form.
Below the term "Elder" (sthavira), the names are listed.

Śāriputra is translated as "Jewel" (珠子) and also as "Body" (身子). Because his mother possessed a beautiful physical form and the marks of intelligence were present in her eyes, he was named after the "jewel" and also after the "body."
The Venerable One was born from a pearl, and is therefore called "Pearl-born" (Muktika).

As for Mahāmaudgalyāyana: *mahā* means "great," and *maudgalyāyana* means "mung bean" (*mudga*) or "pigeon pea" (*caṇaka*). In ancient times there was a rishi who lived in seclusion to pursue his aspirations; he subsisted by gathering these beans. The Venerable One is a descendant of that lineage.
As those of the same clan were numerous, he used "Mahā" (Great) to distinguish him from them.

Mahākāśyapa is translated here as "Great Drinker of Light. Because the light of his body as an ancient seer was so intensely blazing that it swallowed up other lights, rendering them unable to appear, he derived his name and lineage from this.
Kātyāyana, also known as Yaśas, was orphaned at an early age; his mother, out of deep affection for her son, could not remarry and remained like a fan bound by a cord—hence he was given this name.
Kūṭadanta means "Great Knee," so called because his kneecaps were large; he was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra.
Revata means "Constellation," as he was born under this northern lunar mansion after his parents had offered prayers to it.

Cūḷapanthaka means "Slave of Snakes" (Sarpa-dāsa). Alternatively, Cūḷa is translated as "by the side of the great road" and Panthaka as "by the side of the small road," because this Venerable One was born beside a path.
The various sūtras and vinayas refer to Cūḍapanthaka as such.
Nanda means "Joy"; he was originally a cowherd who served the Buddhas while tending cattle. After the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, he subsequently entered the Path.

Ānanda, here translated as "Joyous Celebration," was the Buddha’s maternal cousin. He was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment; because the entire nation rejoiced, he was given the name "Joy."

Rāhula means "obscuration. This is the name of an asura because he is able to obscure the sun and the moon; since this venerable one obstructed the Buddha’s departure from home, just as an asura obscures the moon, he is thus the Tathāgata’s legitimate son.

Gavāmpati is called "the Cow-chewer" (Go-pālaka) and also "the Cow-track" (Gopada); because he was a cow in a past life, his mouth has the habit of chewing like a cow, and his feet have the characteristic marks of cow hooves.

Pindola Bharadvāja is also called Pindolabharadvāja, or Gundupotana; these are all variations of the Sanskrit pronunciation. "Pindola" translates as "Immovable. "Bharadvāja," according to the Tripiṭaka Master Zhendi, translates as "Swift," "Sharp-facultied," or "Broad-spoken"; the *Saṃyukta-avadāna* (Collection of Past Deeds) translates it as "Heavy Banner," as he belonged to one of the eighteen clans of the Brahmins. The Venerable One was of that lineage.
Kālodāyin says it means "black light" or "coarse black," because his physical form was ugly and dark.
Kapphiṇa says it means "the constellation Mūla," because his parents prayed to the Mūla star to obtain a son.
Pūrṇa is called "Good Appearance" because of his excellent countenance and deportment.
Anuruddha is called "Without Poverty" (or "Without Extinction") because he is eternally wealthy.
The following section provides a summary.

Regarding the term "disciple" (*śiṣya*): one is called a "younger brother" (*di*) because they follow after the teacher in their studies; one is called a "son" (*zi*) because their understanding arises from the teacher. The term "brother" manifests the teacher’s humility and deference, while the term "son" clarifies the student’s reverence and veneration.
Together with the various [categories] below, there is the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are three [aspects]: first, the clarification of their types;
II. Listing the Names; III. Summary. Regarding the first section, "Bodhisattva":
*Bodhi* means awakening (*jue*), and *sattva* means sentient being (*zhòngshēng*). This refers to seeking supreme awakening through wisdom while saving sentient beings below through compassion.
The names are listed in Chinese: Mañjuśrī is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode), because his three subtle virtues have partially blossomed.
Regarding the term "Dharma Prince," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The Buddha is the Dharma King; because Bodhisattvas have entered the correct position of the Dharma up to the tenth stage, they are all called Dharma Princes. They are all capable of becoming Buddhas, just like Mañjuśrī."
Ajita means "Unconquerable," because he transcends both the partial and the small [vehicles].
Gandhahasti means "Unceasing," because the correct contemplation of the Middle Way flows into him moment by moment.
"Those who are constantly diligent are free from the two extremes of indolence.
This concludes the summary of such [qualities].
From "Śakra Devānām Indra" downwards refers to the miscellaneous assembly.
The full name is Śakrendra, which translates here as "Capable Lord of Devas" (Neng Tian Di), because he is able to act as the sovereign over all the devas.
The term "and so forth" (etc. includes Brahmā and the World-Protectors (Lokapālas); these are all the foremost among the lords of devas.
"Immeasurable devas" refers to the remaining hosts of celestial beings.
"The great assembly" encompasses humans, asuras, and others in their entirety.
At the conclusion of the sutra, the benefits are summarized as follows:
All those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—heard what the Buddha preached;
thus, it is known that they were present in the assembly.
The new translation lists them all in full at this point.
"From 'At that time' onwards is the second section, the Main Body (Zhengzongfen). It is divided into two parts:
first, the general announcement;"
II. Specific Explanation.
Regarding the initial passage addressed to Śāriputra, this refers to the interlocutor as recorded by the compiler of the sutra.

As for why he addresses a śrāvaka rather than bodhisattvas or devas, the intention is to cause those of the Lesser Vehicle who are at the stage of the initial mind to aspire joyfully to seek rebirth, thereby turning from the Small toward the Great Vehicle.

Śāriputra had already realized the supreme fruit; during the period of the Vaipulya sutras, his bodhicitta had died, and he considered himself to have entered the ultimate nirvana without remainder. From the perspective of the Mahayana, such a state is merely subject to transformation and decay; furthermore, neither of these two paths seeks rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Realm of Common Abode.
Now, as for the Tathāgata’s address, he has bestowed lofty instruction upon those below.
Question:
"If one merely seeks birth in the Small Vehicle at first, can this be called entering the Great [Vehicle]?"
Answer: "The Sūtra says: 'Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"Is this not entering the Great [Vehicle]? From this point downward is the general introductory statement. The first sentence clarifies the distance between them;

the next two sentences clarify the names of the primary and secondary [realms]. The former phrase points to the realm and indicates its name; the latter phrase cites the Buddha’s manifest title. Because it distinguishes [the present] from the past and future, it says "now, in the present dharma."
Below "Śāriputra," there are two parts: first, a general indication; second, a specific exposition. This is divided into two sections:
first, clarifying the adornment of the two types of retribution; [the second follows].
Second, the exhortation to aspire to be born in that land.
This section also has two parts:
first, the secondary retribution (the environment), and second, the primary retribution (the inhabitants).
The first section also has two parts:
first, investigating the name and explaining its meaning;
second, indicating the characteristics by way of retribution.
The first section also has two parts:
first, the inquiry into the name;
second, the explanation of its meaning, beginning with the phrase "In that country... and so forth.
It is called "Ultimate Bliss" because it is contrasted with the Sahā world, which is fully possessed of manifold sufferings; thus it receives the name "Ultimate Bliss.
However, if one discusses it in relation to the four lands, its bliss is not yet ultimate.
Regarding the four lands:
first, the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages, so called because ordinary beings bound by all fetters and sages who have severed their delusions dwell together therein;

second, the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder, so called because those who have practiced the path of expedient means and severed the delusions of the four abodes still possess the remainder of ignorance; thus, they exit the triple world to receive a Dharma-nature body and undergo the birth-and-death of transformation.

Third, the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction: this refers to cultivating the contemplation of the true Middle Way to shatter the delusions of ignorance, thereby attaining birth in that land and receiving the retribution of non-obstructive form and mind.
Fourth, the Land of Constant Quiescent Light: this is the wondrous principle of the nature of the mind; "constant" refers to the Dharma-body;
"quiescent" refers to the Dharma-body, and "quiescent" also refers to liberation.
Light is *prajñā*.
One should know that the former three are phenomena (*dharma*), while the latter one is principle (*tattva*).
The three lands are like images and rice, while the Land of Quiescent Light is like a mirror and a vessel.

If one discusses suffering and bliss individually: because the five turbidities are heavy, it is suffering; because the essence of contemplation is skillful in severing delusions, it is bliss—this refers to the stage of expedient means (*upāya*).

Because one practices and realizes through successive stages, it is suffering; because one enters suddenly through perfect interfusion, it is bliss—this refers to the stage of true reward (*sambhoga-kāya*).
Because partial realization has not yet reached the ultimate, it is suffering; because it is ultimately complete and perfect, it is bliss—this refers to the stage of serene light (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
Regarding the first and last [stages], suffering and bliss are discussed in terms of their results; regarding the middle two, suffering and bliss are explained in relation to their causes.

If viewed in terms of their mutual relationship, then the first seven are all suffering while the final one is exclusively bliss; one should know that it is only the ultimate Land of Peaceful Light (*śāntaprabhā*) that is truly named "Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*).
Because the Buddha intends for all beings to reach the bliss of the eighth stage, he first praises the second stage to cause them to weary of the suffering of the first.
If one attains the second stage and does not regress, then the eighth stage can be expected; such is the skillful means of the Great Sage!
Furthermore, from "Again, Śāriputra" onwards, the second section indicates the characteristics of bliss by way of retribution, which is divided into five parts:
first, the adornment of railings, nets, and rows of trees;
second, the adornment of ponds, waters, and pavilions.
Third, the adornment of golden ground and celestial flowers;
fourth, the adornment of various wondrous birds;
fifth, the adornment of the exquisite sounds of wind-swayed trees. Because of these five adornments, it is called "Experiencing Only Joy."
Regarding the first passage, "railing" (*lángshǔn*) refers to a balustrade; that which runs lengthwise is called a "railing" (*lán*), and that which runs crosswise is called a "crossbar" (*shǔn*).
As for the "four jewels," they are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
2. Adornments of the Ponds and Pavilions.
Regarding the water of eight virtues, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states:
first, it is clear and pure;
Second, it is cool and refreshing;
third, it is sweet and delicious;
fourth, it is light and soft.
5. Moistening; 6. Serene harmony;
7. Relieving hunger and thirst when drunk;
8. Having drunk, one nourishes the sense faculties.
Furthermore, gold and silver are listed below as seven treasures.

Regarding *vaidūrya*—its full name is *vaiḍūrya*, which here is translated as "not far" (*bùyuǎn*). This is because there is a mountain in the Western Regions not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, and since this gem is produced there, it is named accordingly. The original form of the character was written as *liúlí*; later generations changed it to include the "jade" (*yù*) radical.
*Phalī* (crystal) is correctly called *sphāṭika*; its appearance somewhat resembles that of the crystal found in this region, though it exists in two colors:
red and white. *Karketana* (cat's eye), in Sanskrit called *musāragalva*, is translated here as "blue-white precious stone."
The *Shangshu Dazhuan* states:
"Large shells (*dabei*) are like the *qu* of a large carriage; *qu* refers to the carriage-rim (*cheji*).
As for 'red pearls' (*chizhu'), according to the *Fodi lun*, they are produced by red insects, or they are called 'red pearls' because the substance of the pearl itself is red."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Pearls are produced from within the bellies of fish, from within bamboo, and from within the brains of snakes; they do not necessarily arise solely from the womb of oysters.
Regarding *māṇa*, the Sanskrit term is *māṣarāga*, which is translated here as *mǎnǎo*. This jewel is colored like the brain of a horse, and it is named for this reason.
The new edition states:

*Aśmagarbha* means "treasure-vajra" (*zàngchǔ*) or is translated as "womb-treasury" (*tāizàng*). It is named after the solidity of this jewel; its original form was *mǎnǎo* (agate), though later generations added the characters for "stone" or "jade."
In the section below on the ponds, the lotus flowers are clarified through three points:
first, the general indication of their size and shape, as they are like chariot wheels;
second, the indication of their radiant colors, as there are four distinct varieties.
Finally, the fragrance is shown in its entirety, as it is subtle, exquisite, and pure.
Third, the adornment of the golden ground with celestial flowers:
*Mandārava* translates as "pleasing to the mind," because it delights the human heart; because its color is white, it may also be translated as "white flower."
Regarding "yike" (衣裓), ancient commentators explain it as the lapel of a garment.
Paramārtha states:
This refers to the flourishing floral vessels of foreign lands.
Regarding "walking in meditation after eating": this is for the purpose of alleviating fatigue after a meal.
Fourth, the adornment of various wondrous birds, which is further divided into two parts:
I. A clear exposition;
II. An explanation of doubts.
Regarding the first section, there are generally four points:
First, citing the categories;
second, enumerating the names;
third, expounding the sounds.
4. Manifesting Benefits. Regarding the white crane, the *Xianghe jing* (Classic on the Characteristics of Cranes) states:

Its body is naturally pure, hence its color is white; its cry reaches the heavens, hence the crown of its head is red; it feeds upon water, hence its beak is long; it stands upright with its chest forward, hence its hind toes are short; it roosts on land, hence its feet are high and its tail feathers are sparse; it soars through the void, hence its plumage is thick and its flesh is lean; it possesses a large throat to expel the old air and a long neck to take in the new, and thus its life span is immeasurable as it dwells in the heavens.
Regarding the parrot (*śuka*), the *Shanhai jing* states:
"On Mount Huang there is a bird resembling an owl, with green feathers and a red beak; it can speak by licking human tongues, and is called the parrot."
Guo Pu’s commentary states:
"There are those that are white.
*Śāri* is translated here as "spring oriole," or alternatively as "paddybird" (*śarāru*).
The *kalaviṅka*—translated here as "Wondrous Sound"—is so named because even while within its shell, its voice already surpasses that of all other birds.
As for the *jīvañjīvaka* bird, it has two heads on one body; because they possess distinct consciousnesses yet share the same karmic retribution and life-force, it is called "Shared Life."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* calls it the jīvajīvaka; the *Devarāja-sūtra* calls it "born"; and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* calls it gijjha-gijjha—all of these refer to this very bird.
"Jīva" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "living," "being born," or "life. Thus it is known.
"Yayin" (雅音) means "refined and correct.
"Yanchang" (演暢) means "to expound extensively" and "to flow forth with clarity."
The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. That which can produce [virtuous qualities] is called a faculty.
When these same qualities have progressed to the point of being capable and unimpeded, they are called the five powers (*pañcabala*).
The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are called both "factors of awakening" and "limbs"; as various sūtras state, they are the "seven limbs of enlightenment.

The "seven" refers to mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity. Of these, the first [mindfulness] encompasses both concentration and wisdom; the next three [investigation, energy, and joy] are wisdom; and the final three [pliancy, concentration, and equanimity] are concentration.
The Eightfold Noble Path refers to what various sūtras call the Eightfold Right Path.
The eight factors are:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right effort, right concentration, right mindfulness, and right livelihood.
Having heard this sound, [the text] below clarifies the benefits.

Recalling the Buddha is like a king of physicians; recalling the Dharma is like excellent medicine; and recalling the Sangha is like a caregiver. When these three are complete, the disease of afflictions can be cured; this refers specifically to the distinct contemplation of the Three Jewels.

Furthermore, when one turns back to observe one's own mind as quiescent yet constantly illuminating, all phenomena appear vividly; this is mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). When it is illuminating yet constantly quiescent, no dharma can be apprehended; this is called mindfulness of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*). The non-duality of quiescence and illumination is the union of existence and non-existence, and non-existence and existence; this is called mindfulness of the Sangha (*saṃghānusmṛti*). This mindfulness is the Three Jewels of identical essence (*samavastuka-triratna*).

The various birds each understand according to their own kind when a single sound is uttered; therefore, the explanation is given by way of two meanings: distinct characteristics and the same essence.
From "Śāriputra" onwards is the second part, which resolves doubts.

Regarding the first passage: it is intended to address the potential doubt in Śāriputra’s mind that if there are various birds, then there must be the realm of animals—one of the three evil destinies—and since sentient beings undergo birth in the three evil destinies as retribution for their committed transgressions, how can this be called a "Pure Land"?
Therefore, the Buddha rebuked him, saying:
"Do not say that these birds are truly born as a result of karmic retribution.

From the section beginning with "Śāriputra," part two provides an illustration by name to clarify the reality.
Furthermore, in that Pure Land, even the names of the three evil realms do not exist, let alone the actual entities produced by karmic retribution for transgressions!

Question:
"If one regards the body in relation to the land, the body is noble and the land is base; why then do you prioritize the land and place the body last? Answer:
"There are two intentions:"
First, it is for the sake of linguistic convenience: since the names "receptacle" and "sentient beings" refer to the environment and its inhabitants, the land is mentioned first and the body second.
Second, it is for the sake of logical convenience: because the world-system is established first, and only thereafter does a Buddha appear within it.
Regarding the textual analysis, there are two parts:
first, questioning the name and explaining its meaning;

The initial passage has two meanings, hence it receives the name "Immeasurable":
first, immeasurable radiance;

Question:
"The radiance of Śākyamuni can also illuminate immeasurable lands; should he not therefore be named Amitābha? Answer:

"Śākyamuni manifests an inferior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), whose constant radiance extends only one fathom; it is only when he manifests supernatural powers and emits light that it illuminates the immeasurable.
That Buddha manifests a superior response-body, whose constant radiance is immeasurable; therefore, he receives that name."
"Śāriputra," below this, secondly, it clarifies the ten kalpas since his attainment of enlightenment.

2. The adornment of non-retrogression for those born [there].
The previous mention of "adornment" referred to adorning Sukhāvatī; this mention of "adornment" refers to adorning the immeasurable [realms]. Though the words are the same, their meanings differ.
Thus, his disciples are his attendants and those who are living are his subjects; since both of these groups are immeasurable, the Dharma King is named "Immeasurable."
Prior to the aspiration, there are four meanings:
first, radiance; second, lifespan; [and so forth].
Third, disciples;
fourth, those born [in his land]. These four are all immeasurable; therefore, he is named Amitābha.
The former two are based on himself, while the latter two are based on others.
The initial text states that both the disciples of the śrāvakas and the disciples of the bodhisattvas are immeasurable.
As for the śrāvakas, they are so called because they awaken to the Way by hearing the sounds and teachings of the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, from "Again, Śāriputra" onwards is the second [section], the adornment of non-retrogression for those who have been born.
*Avivartika* is translated here as "non-retrogressive. There are three types of non-retrogression:
of stage (*avasthā*), of practice (*caryā*), and of mindfulness (*smṛti*).

In the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), from the first fruit onward up to the stage of Arhat, there is non-retrogression; at the seventh ground, there is non-retrogression in practice; and at the eighth ground, there is non-retrogression in mindfulness.

In the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), these are correlated with the stages of faith, practice, and the candidate for the first ground: at the first ground, one realizes non-retrogression in mindfulness, whereas in the candidate stage one merely cultivates it.

In the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*), from the first to the seventh faith there is non-retrogression in position; from the eighth faith onward, there is non-retrogression in practice; and at the first dwelling (*vihāra*), one realizes non-retrogression in mindfulness.
The Sūtra states that "all [attain it]," which necessarily implies that the meaning encompasses all three stages.
Those in the stage of "one birth remaining" (ekajātipratibaddha) are those at the level of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi).
Since the lifespan in that land is long and the environment is superior, many attain the level of Equal Enlightenment while still in their physical bodies.
*Asaṃkhyeya* is translated as "innumerable.
From the passage beginning with "Śāriputra, those sentient beings who hear [this]" below, there are two parts: second, exhorting them to vow to be born in that land.
The text is divided into three sections:
I. General exhortation;
II. Specific exposition; III.
Conclusion of the meaning.

Regarding the first passage, "sentient beings who hear," this refers to hearing about the aforementioned *pariṣkāra* (environmental support) of Sukhāvatī and the *mūla-āśraya* (primary retribution) of Amitābha.
"Together with all those of superior goodness" means they share that same primary retribution; "assembling together in one place" means they share that same environment.
Below the section on Śāriputra, there is a second part: a detailed exposition. This also has two sections:
first, an indirect clarification (reductio ad absurdum); [second, a direct demonstration].
II. The Actual Demonstration.
Regarding the first passage, the statement that one cannot attain birth through small good deeds serves as a reductio ad absurdum to reveal that one can indeed attain birth through many good deeds.

"Small good deeds" refers to casually making vows or scattered, distracted recitations of the Name; "many good deeds" refers to single-mindedly upholding the Name with a fixed commitment to a specific duration.
Śāriputra, part two: the correct exposition.
This also has four sections:
first, the cultivation of causes;
2. The appearance of the signs;
3. The manifestation of benefits;
4. Attaining birth.

Regarding the initial phrase "grasping and upholding the name": "grasping" (zhi) means to take hold of, and "upholding" (chi) means to maintain. By the power of faith, one takes hold of it so that it is received within the mind; by the power of mindfulness, one maintains it so that it is not forgotten.
"Regarding 'that person,' first is the cause;
second, the signs of response; third, the manifestation of benefits;
and fourth, the attainment of birth."
All is as stated in the text.
Regarding the section beginning with "Śāriputra," the third part is the conclusion of the intent.

As for the statement, "Because I see this benefit, I speak these words," it means that he sees the benefits of that world’s land being the Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), its lifespan being immeasurable, and the adornments of the two types of retribution; thus, he exhorts sentient beings to resolve to be born there, which is why it says, "Therefore, I speak these words."
Below the section on Śāriputra, Part Three: the Distribution Section (Prakaraṇa).
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the Buddha’s exhortation to circulate [the teaching];...
Second, the dispersal of the assembly’s joy.
This section has three parts;
first, the universal praise by all Buddhas.
2. A summary exhortation to be reborn there;
3. An exhortation to believe by citing difficulties.
The first [section] has two parts:
First, the praise of Śākyamuni;
second, the manifestation that all Buddhas are identical.
The first is as explained in the text.
Below the section on the East, the second [section] reveals that all Buddhas are identical.
As for the listing of only the six directions, this is an abbreviation in the Qin edition; the Tang translation, however, includes all ten directions in full.
According to the text, there are six sections, namely the four directions and above and below, each having two parts:
first, the description of that Buddha manifesting signs to indicate [the teaching];
from "You all" onwards, second, the demonstration of that Buddha speaking words to encourage faith.
"Akṣobhya" means "Immovable" in this language, because he is not moved by the two extremes; he extends his broad and long tongue to manifest that he is free from falsehood.
When it says, "You sentient beings should have faith," and so forth, it is an exhortation to believe in this sutra.
"Praising until one is protected by the Buddhas" is an alternative title for this sutra.
The name "Sutra on Praising the Pure Land" used in the Tang translation is precisely based on this text, as it praises inconceivable merit.

Śākyamuni spoke of Amitābha’s primary and secondary marks, which are protected and remembered by all Buddhas; he manifested that the Buddhas of the ten directions all rejoice in and protect them, thereby ensuring that celestial Māras cannot disturb the mindfulness [of the practitioner] and causing those who have faith not to regress from Bodhi.
"Sun, Moon, and Lamp" is a metaphor for the three types of wisdom.
"Renowned Light" means that his fame is heard everywhere, like light shining universally.
"Great Flame Shoulder" indicates that the shoulders represent the two [other] types of wisdom, while the flames represent the illumination of principle.

Regarding "Sumeru Lamp": Sumeru means "Wondrously High" (*Miaogao*). "Wondrous" signifies the perfect fusion of the three wisdoms; "High" signifies transcending the stage of causes; and "Lamp" serves as a metaphor for the universal illumination of these three wisdoms.
"Difficult to thwart" means that when one internally realizes the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one cannot be defeated by the four māras.
"Net-light" (*Jālinīprabha*) refers to the light of wisdom being like a net that universally covers the ten realms. *Dharma* is translated here as "dharma";

since it is connected below with "dharma-banner" (*dharmadhvaja*) and "upholding the dharma" (*dharmadharin*), the Sanskrit term is retained to distinguish the phrasing. These three names seem to represent the three truths: "dharma" is the empty truth (*śūnyatā-satya*), tranquil and worthy of following; "dharma-banner" is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), where the illuminator can be seen; and "upholding the dharma" is the middle way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), which simultaneously maintains both extremes.
"Adorned with a body of variegated jewel-flowers" means that the essence of the Buddha-fruit is adorned by the flowers of the causes of the ten thousand practices.
"Sāla" here translates as "firm and solid.
Śāriputra, within your own mind, [the second point] concludes the exhortation to be reborn there.
Furthermore, there are two parts:
first, the benefits of hearing the sūtra;
second, clarifying the efficacy of the vow for rebirth.
The first section also has three parts:
first, citing different names to raise a question;
second, from "Śāriputra" onwards, clarifying the benefits based on the sūtra and the Buddha.

*Anuttara* means "unsurpassed" (*wu-shang*); *samyak* means "correct" (*zheng*), while *san* (from *samyak*) means "equal" (*deng*); and *bodhi* means "awakening" (*jue*). Because the ultimate fruit transcends its causes, it is called "unsurpassed. "Correct" refers to the correct contemplation of the Middle Way; "equal" refers to the simultaneous illumination of both extremes. This constitutes the threefold wisdom within a single mind on the level of fruition.
Below this, third, is the summary that exhorts one to believe in both.
Below the passage beginning with "Śāriputra," second, is the clarification of the merit of aspiring for rebirth.
This also has two parts:
The first section sets forth the aspiration to manifest benefit.

Regarding the phrase "those who have already arisen" and so forth: those who have already made the vow in the past have already arisen; those who are making the vow now in the present have arisen now; and those who shall make the vow in the future will arise then.
Therefore, the section below [the passage beginning with] "Second," summarizes the exhortation based on faith;
for in the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, faith is that by which one enters, and wisdom is that by which one crosses over.
The section beginning with "Śāriputra," third, cites difficult cases to encourage faith.
Furthermore, there are two parts:
first, clarifying that I praise them;
second, clarifying that they praise me.
Regarding the first section, the praise offered here refers precisely to the six directions just mentioned.
Below that, the second part clarifies how they praise me. This also has two sub-sections:
First, the citation of his praise;
second, the manifestation of its non-falsity.

Regarding the first passage: Śākyamuni is translated as "Capable Benevolent One" (Nengren), and Muni as "Silent Sage" (Jimo). "Capable Benevolent One" signifies great compassion responding to sentient beings, while "Silent Sage" signifies great wisdom merging with the principle.

Those who are able to perform deeds that are extremely difficult and rare do two things: first, they attain enlightenment within the five turbidities; second, they preach the Dharma, which is difficult to believe, for the sake of sentient beings.
*Sahā* means "endurance," because sentient beings therein are capable of enduring and bearing the three poisons.

Regarding the "impurity of the eon" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*): in Sanskrit, *kalpa* means "time-period. Because the other four impurities gather together during this time, it is called the "impurity of the eon. Regarding the "impurity of views" (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*):
these are the five sharp afflictions, namely the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
The turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) refers to the five dull underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), namely greed, hatred, and so forth.

The turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) is a provisional designation established based on the acquisition of sharp or dull karmic retributions. The shortening of years and the hastening of the life span is called the turbidity of life (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*).
Generally speaking, "turbidity" is like throwing sand and soil into clear water: the soil loses its distinctness as it rises, while the water loses its purity, becoming turbid and murky.
Now, due to these five turbidities, the water of principle loses its clarity.

To speak of this dharma that is difficult to believe means to say that by reciting the Name for a single day, one will at the end of life be reborn in Sukhāvatī and attain non-retrogressive bodhi; that such a benefit is obtained through these meager roots of goodness is what makes it difficult to believe.

Thus, ordinary beings and sages are equal, with no distinction of high or low; when the mind is pure, the land is pure, transcending [the world] in an instant. It is extremely easy to believe that one will be born in Sukhāvatī, yet because delusion is profound and attachments are heavy, they hear it and do not accept it; therefore, it is said to be difficult to believe.
Śāriputra, the second section concludes that [the teaching] is not in vain.

Regarding the phrase "this is exceedingly difficult": it is already difficult to attain bodhi while practicing difficult deeds within a world-system of the five turbidities; furthermore, to preach this dharma which is difficult to believe—performing both tasks simultaneously—is truly exceedingly difficult.
The Buddhas have praised me; how could their words be empty?
Following the Buddha’s teaching, secondly, the assembly rejoices and disperses.
Asuras are called "non-gods" (*asura*); although they enjoy wealth and pleasure like the gods, they possess much flattery and deception and lack divine conduct, and thus they receive that name.
Having heard what had never been heard before, he received it with joy and faith.
Out of reverence for the Dharma and respect for the Teacher, he prostrated himself and departed.
*Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*.
